danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 25
paragraphs: På Lysye Gory (Skaldet Bjerg), fyrst Nikolaj Andrejevitj Bolkonskijs gods, ventede man dagligt den unge fyrst Andrej og hans hustru, men denne forventning forstyrrede ikke den faste daglige rytme i den gamle fyrstes husholdning. Generalløjtnant fyrst Nikolaj Andrejevitj — i selskabslivet kaldet »Preussens Konge« — havde, lige siden kejser Poul forviste ham til sit landgods, boet der uafbrudt med sin datter, fyrstinde Marja, og hendes selskabsdame, frøken Bourienne. Selvom han under den nye kejsers styre frit kunne vende tilbage til hovedstæderne, blev han boende på landet og bemærkede, at enhver, der ønskede at se ham, kunne rejse de hundrede verst fra Moskva til Lysye Gory, mens han selv ikke havde brug for nogen eller noget. Han plejede at sige, at der kun findes to kilder til menneskelig last — dovenskab og overtro — og kun to dyder — virksomhed og forstand. Han påtog sig selv sin datters uddannelse, og for at udvikle disse to hoveddyder gav han hende undervisning i algebra og geometri, indtil hun var tyve, og tilrettelagde hendes liv, så al hendes tid var optaget. Han selv var altid beskæftiget: han skrev sine memoirer, løste opgaver i højere matematik, drejede snustobaksdåser på en drejebænk, arbejdede i haven eller førte tilsyn med de byggerier, der altid var i gang på godset. Da regelmæssighed er en grundbetingelse for virksomhed, var regelmæssigheden i hans husholdning drevet til det yderste. Han kom altid til bords under nøjagtig de samme vilkår, og ikke blot på den samme time, men på det samme minut. Over for alle omkring ham, fra datteren til de livegne, var fyrsten skarp og ubetinget krævende, så at han uden at være et hjerteløst menneske indgød en frygt og ærbødighed, som få hjerteløse mennesker ville have vakt. Selvom han var pensioneret og nu ikke havde nogen indflydelse på politiske forhold, anså enhver højtstående embedsmand, der blev udnævnt til den provins, hvor fyrstens gods lå, det for sin pligt at aflægge ham besøg og ventede i det høje forværelse, ligesom arkitekten, gartneren eller fyrstinde Marja gjorde, til fyrsten viste sig præcist på det aftalte tidspunkt. Alle, der sad i dette forværelse, oplevede den samme følelse af ærbødighed og endda frygt, når den umådeligt høje dør til studereværelset åbnede sig og viste skikkelsen af en ret lille, gammel mand med pudret paryk, små visne hænder og buskede grå øjenbryn, der, når han rynkede dem, undertiden skjulte glimt af hans kloge, ungdommeligt funklende øjne.

Den morgen, da det unge par skulle ankomme, gik fyrstinde Marja som sædvanligt ind i forværelset til den faste tid for morgenhilsenen, korsede sig ængsteligt og bad en stille bøn. Hver morgen kom hun på denne måde, og hver morgen bad hun om, at det daglige møde måtte gå godt.
En gammel, pudret tjener, der sad i forværelset, rejste sig stille og sagde hviskende: »Vær så venlig at gå ind.«

Igennem døren hørtes den regelmæssige summen af en drejebænk. Fyrstinden åbnede forsigtigt døren, der bevægede sig lydløst og let. Hun standsede ved indgangen. Fyrsten arbejdede ved drejebænken og kiggede op efter et flygtigt blik, men fortsatte sit arbejde.

Det enorme studereværelse var fyldt med ting, der tydeligvis var i stadig brug. Det store bord dækket af bøger og planer, de høje, glaslågede bogskabe med nøgler i låsene, det høje stående skrivebord med en opslået notesbog, og drejebænken med værktøj liggende parat og spåner spredt omkring — alt vidnede om en uafbrudt, alsidig og velordnet virksomhed. Den lille fods bevægelse i en sølvbroderet tartarstøvle og det faste tryk af den magre, senede hånd vidnede om, at fyrsten stadig besad den seje udholdenhed og livskraft, der hører en robust alderdom til. Efter nogle få omdrejninger mere tog han foden fra pedalen, tørrede sin mejsel af, lagde den i en læderpung fastgjort til drejebænken og gik hen mod bordet, hvor han tilkaldte sin datter. Han gav aldrig sine børn sin velsignelse, så han rakte simpelthen sin stride kind (endnu ubarberet) frem og sagde, mens han betragtede hende ømt og opmærksomt, med streng stemme:
»Helt frisk? Godt, sæt dig så.« Han tog notesbogen med geometrilektioner, som han selv havde skrevet, og trak en stol hen med foden.
»Til i morgen!« sagde han, fandt hurtigt den rette side og markerede med en hård negl fra det ene afsnit til det næste.
Fyrstinden bøjede sig over notesbogen på bordet.
»Vent, her er et brev til dig,« sagde den gamle mand pludselig og trak et brev i kvindehandskrift ud af en pose, der hang over bordet, og kastede det ned til hende.
Ved synet af brevet viste røde pletter sig i fyrstindens ansigt. Hun greb det hurtigt og bøjede hovedet over det.
»Fra Héloïse?« spurgte fyrsten med et koldt smil, der viste hans stadig sunde, gullige tænder.
»Ja, det er fra Julie,« svarede fyrstinden med et sky blik og et forsagt smil.
»Jeg lader to breve mere passere, men det tredje læser jeg,« sagde fyrsten strengt; »jeg er bange for, at du skriver en masse vrøvl. Det tredje læser jeg!«
»Læs gerne dette, Far,« sagde fyrstinden og rødmede endnu mere, mens hun rakte ham brevet.
»Det tredje, sagde jeg, det tredje!« råbte fyrsten brat, skubbede brevet væk og trak med albuerne på bordet notesbogen med de geometriske figurer hen til sig.

»Nå, frue,« begyndte han, bøjede sig over bogen tæt ved sin datter og lagde en arm på stolens ryg, så hun følte sig omgivet fra alle sider af den skarpe duft af alderdom og tobak, som hun kendte så godt. »Nå, frue, disse trekanter er ens; vær venlig at bemærke, at vinkel ABC...«

Fyrstinden kiggede rædselsslagne ind i sin fars øjne, der funklede tæt ved hende; de røde pletter i hendes ansigt kom og gik, og det var tydeligt, at hun intet forstod og var så bange, at frygten ville hindre hende i at forstå nogen af sin fars videre forklaringer, hvor klare de end måtte være. Hvad enten det var lærerens eller elevens skyld, gentog det samme sig hver dag: fyrstindens øjne blev matte, hun kunne hverken se eller høre noget, men var kun bevidst om sin strenge fars visnede ansigt tæt ved sig, hans ånde og lugten af ham, og kunne kun tænke på, hvordan hun hurtigst muligt kom væk til sit eget værelse for i fred at løse opgaven. Den gamle mand var ude af sig selv: han rykkede stolen, han sad på, støjende frem og tilbage, anstrengte sig for at beherske sig og ikke blive heftig, men blev det næsten altid, skældte ud og smed undertiden notesbogen fra sig.
Fyrstinden gav et forkert svar.
»Jamen, er hun ikke en tåbe!« råbte fyrsten, skubbede bogen til side og vendte sig brat om; men han rejste sig straks, vandrede frem og tilbage, rørte let ved sin datters hår og satte sig igen.
Han trak sin stol hen til bordet og fortsatte sin forklaring.

»Det duer ikke, fyrstinde; det duer ikke,« sagde han, da fyrstinde Marja havde taget notesbogen med næste dags lektion og lukket den og var ved at gå: »Matematikken er det vigtigste, frue! Jeg vil ikke have, at du skal ligne vores dumme damer. Væn dig til det, så kommer du til at holde af det,« og han klappede hende på kinden. »Det driver alt vrøvlet ud af hovedet.«
Hun vendte sig for at gå, men han standsede hende med en gestus og tog en uopskåret bog fra det høje skrivebord.
»Her er en slags Mysteriernes Nøgle, som din Héloïse har sendt dig. Religiøst! Jeg blander mig ikke i nogens tro ... Jeg har kigget i den. Tag den. Nå, gå nu. Gå.«
Han klappede hende på skulderen og lukkede selv døren efter hende.

Fyrstinde Marja gik tilbage til sit værelse med det triste, ængstelige udtryk, der sjældent forlod hende, og som gjorde hendes blege, sygelige ansigt endnu mere blegt. Hun satte sig ved sit skrivebord, hvorpå der stod miniatureportrætter, og som flød med bøger og papirer. Fyrstinden var lige så uordentlig, som hendes far var ordentlig. Hun lagde geometribogen ned og brød ivrigt brevets segl. Det var fra hendes mest fortrolige barndomsveninde; den samme Julie Karagina, der havde været med til Rostov-familiens navnedagsfest.
Julie skrev på fransk:

Kære, dyrebare veninde! Hvor forfærdelig og skrækkelig adskillelsen er! Selvom jeg siger til mig selv, at halvdelen af mit liv og min lykke er knyttet til dig, og at vore hjerter trods afstanden er forenet af ubrydelige bånd, gør mit hjerte dog oprør mod skæbnen, og trods glæderne og adspredelserne omkring mig kan jeg ikke overvinde en vis hemmelig sorg, der har fyldt mit hjerte, lige siden vi skiltes. Hvorfor er vi ikke sammen som i sidste sommer, i dit store studereværelse, på den blå sofa, fortrolighedens sofa? Hvorfor kan jeg ikke nu, som for tre måneder siden, hente ny moralsk styrke fra dit blik, så mildt, roligt og indtrængende — et blik, jeg holdt så meget af, og som jeg synes at se for mig, mens jeg skriver?

Da fyrstinde Marja havde læst så langt, sukkede hun og kastede et blik i spejlet, der stod til højre for hende. Det genspejlede en spinkel, unådefuld skikkelse og et tyndt ansigt. Hendes øjne, altid triste, kiggede nu med særlig håbløshed på hendes spejlbillede. »Hun smigrer mig,« tænkte fyrstinden og vendte sig bort for at læse videre. Men Julie smigrede ikke sin veninde. Fyrstindens øjne — store, dybe og strålende (det var, som om der til tider udgik varme lysstråler fra dem) — var så smukke, at de trods hendes ansigts mangel på skønhed ofte gav hende en tiltrækning, der var stærkere end selve skønheden. Men fyrstinden så aldrig det smukke udtryk i sine egne øjne — det blik, de havde, når hun ikke tænkte på sig selv. Som hos alle antog hendes ansigt et anstrengt, unaturligt udtryk, så snart hun kiggede i et spejl. Hun læste videre:

Hele Moskva taler kun om krig. En af mine to brødre er allerede i udlandet, den anden er ved garden, som er på marchen mod grænsen. Vor kære kejser har forladt Petersborg, og man mener, han agter at udsætte sin dyrebare person for krigens farer. Gid den korsikanske uhyre, der ødelægger freden i Europa, må blive styrtet af den engel, som den Almægtige i Sin godhed har givet os til hersker! For slet ikke at tale om mine brødre har denne krig berøvet mig et af de venskaber, der ligger mit hjerte nærmest. Jeg mener den unge Nikolaj Rostov, der med sin entusiasme ikke kunne holde ud at være uvirksom og har forladt universitetet for at gå ind i hæren. Jeg vil tilstå for dig, kære Marja, at trods hans store ungdom var hans afrejse til hæren en stor sorg for mig. Denne unge mand, som jeg fortalte dig om i sommer, er så ædelt sindet og besidder den ægte ungdommelighed, man sjældent finder hos vore gamle mænd på tyve; og han er frem for alt så oprigtig og har så meget hjerte. Han er så ren og poetisk, at mit bekendtskab med ham, hvor flygtigt det end var, har været en af de sødeste trøster for mit stakkels hjerte, der allerede har lidt så meget. En dag skal jeg fortælle dig om vores afsked og alt, hvad der blev sagt. Det er endnu for nyt. Åh, kære veninde, du er lykkelig, der ikke kender disse bitre glæder og sorger. Du er heldig, for sorgerne er som regel de stærkeste! Jeg ved meget vel, at grev Nikolaj er for ung til nogensinde at blive mere for mig end en ven, men dette søde venskab, dette poetiske og rene samvær, var det, mit hjerte behøvede. Men nok om det! Den store nyhed, som hele Moskva sladrer om, er den gamle grev Bezukhovs død og hans arv. Tænk! De tre prinsesser har fået meget lidt, fyrst Vasilij ingenting, og det er monsieur Pierre, der har arvet hele ejendommen og desuden er blevet anerkendt som legitim; så han er nu grev Bezukhov og ejer af den største formue i Rusland. Man siger, at fyrst Vasilij spillede en meget uværdig rolle i denne sag og vendte meget forkølet tilbage til Petersborg.

Jeg må tilstå, at jeg forstår meget lidt af alle disse sager med testamenter og arv; men det ved jeg, at siden denne unge mand, som vi alle kendte som den jævne monsieur Pierre, er blevet grev Bezukhov og ejer af en af de største formuer i Rusland, morer det mig storligt at iagttage ændringen i tone og manerer hos mødrene, tynget af giftefærdige døtre, og hos de unge damer selv, over for ham, selvom han, mellem os sagt, altid har forekommet mig at være en stakkels fyr. Da man i de sidste to år har moret sig med at finde ægtemænd til mig (de fleste kender jeg ikke engang), omtaler Moskvas ægteskabskrøniker mig nu som den kommende grevinde Bezukhova. Men du vil forstå, at jeg ikke har noget ønske om den post. Apropos ægteskaber: ved du, at for nylig fortalte den altomfattende tante Anna Mikhajlovna mig under løfte om streng hemmelighed om en giftermålsplan for dig? Det er hverken mere eller mindre end med fyrst Vasilijs søn Anatol (Kuragin), som de ønsker at reformere ved at gifte ham med en rig og fornem kvinde, og det er dig, hans slægtninges valg er faldet på. Jeg ved ikke, hvad du tænker om det, men jeg anser det for min pligt at lade dig vide det. Han siges at være meget smuk og en forfærdelig vildbasse. Det er alt, hvad jeg har kunnet finde ud af om ham.

Men nok sladder. Jeg er ved enden af mit andet ark papir, og Mamma har sendt bud efter mig til middag hos Apraksin-familien. Læs den mystiske bog, jeg sender dig; den har enorm succes her. Selvom den indeholder ting, der er svære for den svage menneskelige forstand at begribe, er det en beundringsværdig bog, der beroliger og løfter sjælen. Farvel! Hils hr. din fader og bring min kompliment til frøken Bourienne. Jeg omfavner dig, som jeg elsker dig.
JULIE
P.S. Fortæl mig nyt om din bror og hans charmerende lille kone.

Fyrstinden sad en stund eftertænksomt med et smil, og hendes strålende øjne lyste op, så hendes ansigt blev fuldstændig forvandlet. Så rejste hun sig pludselig og gik med sine tunge skridt hen til bordet. Hun tog et ark papir, og hendes hånd fløj hurtigt hen over det. Dette var hendes svar, også på fransk:

Kære, dyrebare veninde! Dit brev af den 13. har beredt mig stor glæde. Så du elsker mig stadig, min romantiske Julie? Adskillelsen, som du taler så ilde om, synes ikke at have haft sin sædvanlige virkning på dig. Du klager over vores adskillelse. Hvad skulle jeg da sige, om jeg vovede at klage, jeg, der er berøvet alle, som er mig kære? Åh, hvis vi ikke havde religionen til at trøste os, ville livet være meget trist. Hvorfor mener du, at jeg skulle se strengt på din hengivenhed for den unge mand? I sådanne sager er jeg kun streng mod mig selv. Jeg forstår sådanne følelser hos andre, og skønt jeg aldrig har følt dem og derfor ikke kan billige dem, fordømmer jeg dem heller ikke. Blot forekommer det mig, at den kristne kærlighed, kærligheden til næsten, kærligheden til fjenden, er mere værdig, sødere og bedre end de følelser, en ung mands smukke øjne kan vække hos en romantisk og kærlig ung pige som dig.

Nyheden om grev Bezukhovs død nåede os før dit brev, og min far var meget berørt af den. Han siger, at greven var den næstsidste repræsentant for det store århundrede, og at det nu er hans egen tur, men at han vil gøre alt for at lade sin tur komme så sent som muligt. Gud bevare os fra den forfærdelige ulykke!

Jeg kan ikke være enig med dig om Pierre, som jeg kendte som barn. Han har altid forekommet mig at have et udmærket hjerte, og det er den egenskab, jeg sætter højest hos mennesker. Hvad angår hans arv og fyrst Vasilijs rolle, er det meget trist for dem begge. Åh, min kære veninde, vor guddommelige Frelsers ord om, at det er lettere for en kamel at gå gennem et nåleøje end for en rig mand at komme ind i Guds rige — de er forfærdelig sande. Jeg ynker fyrst Vasilij, men har endnu mere ondt af Pierre. Så ung og belastet med sådanne rigdomme — for hvilke fristelser vil han ikke blive udsat! Hvis man spurgte mig, hvad jeg ønsker mest af alt på jorden, ville det være at være fattigere end den fattigste tigger. Tusind tak, kære veninde, for det bind, du har sendt mig, og som har så stor succes i Moskva. Men da du fortæller mig, at det ved siden af gode ting indeholder andet, som vor svage menneskelige forstand ikke kan begribe, forekommer det mig temmelig nytteløst at bruge tid på at læse, hvad der er ubegribeligt og derfor ikke kan bære frugt. Jeg har aldrig kunnet forstå den forkærlighed, nogle mennesker har for at forvirre deres sind ved at fordybe sig i mystiske bøger, der blot vækker tvivl og ophidser fantasien og giver dem en hang til overdrivelse, der er ganske i modstrid med kristen enfold. Lad os hellere læse apostlenes breve og evangelierne. Lad os ikke søge at gennemtrænge de mysterier, de indeholder; for hvordan kan vi, elendige syndere som vi er, kende de forfærdelige og hellige hemmeligheder hos Forsynet, mens vi forbliver i dette kød, der danner et uigennemtrængeligt slør mellem os og det Evige? Lad os hellere holde os til at studere de sublime regler, vor guddommelige Frelser har efterladt os til vejledning her på jorden. Lad os forsøge at følge dem, og lad os overbevise os selv om, at jo mindre vi lader vore svage menneskelige tanker flakke, des mere vil vi behage Gud, som forkaster al viden, der ikke kommer fra Ham; og jo mindre vi søger at fatte det, Han har fundet for godt at skjule for os, desto snarere vil Han åbenbare det for os gennem Sin guddommelige Ånd.

Min far har ikke talt til mig om en bejler, men har kun fortalt mig, at han har modtaget et brev og venter besøg af fyrst Vasilij. Hvad angår dette giftermålsforslag for mig, vil jeg sige dig, kære, søde veninde, at jeg betragter ægteskabet som en guddommelig institution, vi må bøje os for. Hvor smertefuldt det end måtte være for mig — skulle den Almægtige pålægge mig en hustrus og moders pligter, vil jeg forsøge at opfylde dem så trofast, jeg kan, uden at ængste mig med at granske mine følelser for den, Han måtte give mig til ægtefælle.

Jeg har fået brev fra min bror, der bebuder sin snarlige ankomst til Lysye Gory med sin hustru. Denne glæde bliver dog kun kort, for han rejser igen for at deltage i denne ulykkelige krig, som vi er blevet draget ind i, Gud ved hvordan eller hvorfor. Ikke blot der, hvor du er — midt i begivenhedernes og verdens centrum — er der kun tale om krig, selv her midt i markarbejde og den naturens ro, som byfolk anser for karakteristisk for landet, høres og føles krigsrygternes smerte. Min far taler kun om marcher og modmarcher, ting jeg intet forstår af; og i forgårs, på min daglige spadseretur gennem landsbyen, var jeg vidne til en hjerteskærende scene ... Det var et hold værnepligtige, udskrevet blandt vore folk, på vej for at slutte sig til hæren. Du skulle have set tilstanden hos mødrene, konerne og børnene til de mænd, der drog af sted, og have hørt hulkene. Det synes, som om menneskeheden har glemt vor guddommelige Frelsers love, der prædikede kærlighed og tilgivelse af uret — og at mennesker tilskriver den største fortjeneste til dygtighed i at slå hinanden ihjel.
Farvel, kære og venlige veninde; gid vor guddommelige Frelser og Hans allerhelligste Moder have dig i deres hellige og almægtige varetægt!
MARJA

»Åh, du sender et brev af sted, fyrstinde? Jeg har allerede afsendt mit. Jeg har skrevet til min stakkels moder,« sagde den smilende frøken Bourienne hurtigt med sin behagelige, bløde stemme med det rullende r. Hun bragte ind i fyrstinde Marjas anstrengte, sørgmodige og mørke verden en helt anden atmosfære — sorgløs, munter og selvtilfreds.

»Fyrstinde, jeg må advare Dem,« tilføjede hun med dæmpet stemme og tydeligvis nydende lyden af sin egen røst, med overdreven grasseyen, »fyrsten har skældt ud på Mikhail Ivanovitj. Han er i meget dårligt humør — meget gnaven. Vær forberedt.«
»Åh, kære veninde,« svarede fyrstinde Marja, »jeg har bedt dig om aldrig at advare mig om min fars humør. Jeg tillader ikke mig selv at dømme ham og ville ikke have, at andre gør det.«

Fyrstinden kiggede på sit ur og opdagede, at hun var fem minutter forsinket med sin øvelse på klavichorden, og gik ind i dagligstuen med et uroligt blik. Mellem tolv og to, som dagsprogrammet fastsatte, hvilede fyrsten, og fyrstinden spillede klavichord.

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: At Bald Hills, the estate of Prince Nikolai Andreevich Bolkonsky, the arrival of young Prince Andrei and his wife was expected any day, but this didn't disrupt the old prince's rigid household routine. General-in-Chief Prince Nikolai Andreevich—nicknamed "the King of Prussia" in society—had been living at his country estate continuously since Emperor Paul had exiled him there, together with his daughter, Princess Mary, and her companion, Mademoiselle Bourienne. Though the new reign had made him free to return to the capitals, he continued to live in the country, remarking that anyone who wanted to see him could make the hundred-mile trip from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed nobody and nothing. He liked to say there are only two sources of human vice—idleness and superstition—and only two virtues—activity and intelligence. He personally oversaw his daughter's education, and to develop these two virtues in her, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty and organized her life so that every hour was accounted for. He himself was perpetually busy: writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on a lathe, working in the garden, or supervising the construction that was always underway on his estate. Since regularity is the first condition of productivity, regularity in his household was maintained to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter down to the servants, the prince was sharp and unfailingly demanding—not out of cruelty, but with a severity that inspired the kind of fear and respect that few genuinely cruel men could have commanded. Although he was retired and no longer wielded political influence, every senior official appointed to the province felt duty-bound to pay him a visit, and they waited in his lofty antechamber—alongside the architect, the gardener, and Princess Mary—until the prince appeared at precisely the appointed time. Everyone in that waiting room experienced the same mix of respect and dread when the enormously tall study door swung open to reveal the small figure of the old man: powdered wig, small withered hands, and bushy gray eyebrows that, when he frowned, could hide the sharp gleam of his youthful, piercing eyes.

On the morning of the day the young couple was expected, Princess Mary entered the antechamber at the usual time for the morning greeting, crossing herself nervously and repeating a silent prayer. She came in like this every morning, and every morning she prayed the encounter would go smoothly.
An old powdered manservant sitting in the antechamber stood quietly and said in a whisper: "Please go in."

Through the door came the steady hum of a lathe. The princess timidly pushed open the door, which moved silently on its hinges. She paused at the threshold. The prince was working at the lathe and, after a quick glance, went on with what he was doing.

The enormous study was full of objects clearly in constant use. A large table strewn with books and plans, tall glass-fronted bookcases with keys in their locks, a high standing desk with an open exercise book on it, the lathe with tools at the ready and shavings scattered around—everything spoke of continuous, varied, disciplined activity. The rhythmic motion of his small foot in a silver-embroidered Tartar boot, and the firm pressure of his lean, sinewy hand, showed that the prince still possessed all the endurance and energy of a hardy old age. After a few more turns of the lathe, he removed his foot from the pedal, wiped his chisel, dropped it into a leather pouch attached to the lathe, and walked to the table to greet his daughter. He never gave his children a blessing, so he simply offered his bristly, unshaven cheek and, looking at her with tender attention, said sternly:
"Feeling well? Good. Sit down." He took the exercise book of geometry lessons he had written himself and pulled up a chair with his foot.
"For tomorrow!" he said, quickly finding the right page and marking a section with a hard fingernail, scratching from one paragraph to the next.
The princess bent over the exercise book on the table.
"Wait—here's a letter for you," the old man said suddenly, pulling a letter in a woman's handwriting from a bag hanging above the table and tossing it to her.
Red blotches appeared on the princess's face at the sight of the letter. She snatched it up quickly and bent her head over it.
"From Heloise?" the prince asked with a cold smile that revealed his still-sound, yellowish teeth.
"Yes, it's from Julie," the princess replied with a timid glance and a shy smile.
"I'll let two more letters pass, but the third one I'm reading," the prince said sternly. "I'm afraid you write a lot of nonsense. I'll read the third!"
"Read this one if you like, Father," said the princess, blushing even more and holding out the letter.
"The third, I said the third!" the prince snapped, pushing the letter away. He leaned his elbows on the table and drew the geometry exercise book toward him.

"Now then, young lady," he began, bending over the book close to his daughter and resting his arm on the back of her chair, so that she found herself enveloped on all sides by the sharp scent of old age and tobacco that she had known all her life. "Now then—these triangles are equal. Please observe that the angle ABC..."

The princess stared with frightened eyes at her father's face, which glittered with intensity right next to hers. The red patches came and went on her cheeks, and it was obvious she understood nothing and was so terrified that her fear would block any comprehension of his explanations, no matter how clear. Whether the fault lay with the teacher or the student, the same thing happened every day: the princess's eyes glazed over, she could neither see nor hear, conscious only of her stern father's withered face close to hers, his breath and his smell, able to think of nothing but escaping to her own room to work out the problem in peace. The old man would lose his composure, noisily shoving his chair back and forth, struggling to hold his temper—and nearly always failing. He would scold her, and sometimes hurl the exercise book across the room.
The princess gave a wrong answer.
"Now, isn't she a fool!" the prince shouted, shoving the book aside and turning sharply away. But he immediately stood up, paced the room, gently touched his daughter's hair, and sat down again.
He pulled his chair closer and resumed his explanation.

"This won't do, Princess, it won't do," he said as Princess Mary closed the exercise book with tomorrow's lesson and prepared to leave. "Mathematics is essential, young lady! I don't want you turning out like those silly society women. Stick with it and you'll come to enjoy it." He patted her cheek. "It'll drive all the foolishness out of your head."
She turned to go, but he stopped her with a gesture and took an uncut book from the high desk.
"Here's some sort of Key to the Mysteries that your Heloise sent you. Religion! I don't interfere with anyone's beliefs... I've had a look at it. Take it. Well—go on, go."
He patted her on the shoulder and personally closed the door behind her.

Princess Mary returned to her room wearing the sad, anxious expression that rarely left her face and that made her plain, sickly features seem even plainer. She sat down at her writing desk, which was surrounded by miniature portraits and cluttered with books and papers. The princess was as messy as her father was orderly. She set down the geometry book and eagerly broke the seal on her letter. It was from her closest childhood friend—the very same Julie Karagina who had been at the Rostovs' name-day party.
Julie wrote in French:

Dear and precious Friend, How terrible and frightening it is to be separated! Though I tell myself that half my life and half my happiness are wrapped up in you, and that despite the distance between us our hearts are joined by unbreakable bonds, my heart rebels against fate, and despite all the pleasures and distractions around me, I cannot shake a certain secret sorrow that has lived in my heart ever since we parted. Why can't we be together as we were last summer, in your big study, on the blue sofa—the sofa where we shared our secrets? Why can't I draw fresh moral strength from your gaze, as I did three months ago—that gaze so gentle, calm, and searching, which I loved so much and seem to see before me now as I write?

Having read this far, Princess Mary sighed and glanced at the mirror on her right. It reflected a thin, graceless figure and a gaunt face. Her eyes, always sad, now looked with particular hopelessness at her own reflection. "She flatters me," the princess thought, looking away and continuing to read. But Julie was not flattering her friend. The princess's eyes—large, deep, and luminous, as though warm shafts of light sometimes radiated from them—were so beautiful that despite the plainness of her face, they often lent her a magnetism more powerful than conventional beauty. But the princess never saw the beautiful expression of her own eyes—the look they had when she wasn't thinking about herself. Like everyone, her face took on a forced, unnatural expression as soon as she looked in a mirror. She continued reading:

All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are about to march for the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg, and it's believed he intends to expose his precious person to the dangers of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is destroying the peace of Europe may be overthrown by the angel whom the Almighty, in His goodness, has given us as our sovereign! To say nothing of my brothers, this war has robbed me of one of the bonds dearest to my heart. I mean young Nikolai Rostov, who was so passionately enthusiastic that he couldn't bear to remain idle and has left the university to join the army. I will confess to you, dear Mary, that despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army was a great sorrow for me. This young man, of whom I told you last summer, is so noble-spirited and full of that genuine youthfulness one so rarely finds anymore among our old men of twenty—and above all, he is so honest and has so much heart. He is so pure and poetic that my relationship with him, brief as it was, has been one of the sweetest comforts to my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. Someday I'll tell you about our parting and everything that was said. It's all still too fresh. Ah, dear friend, you're lucky not to know these sharp joys and sorrows. You are fortunate, because the sorrows are usually stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nikolai is too young ever to be more than a friend to me, but this sweet friendship, this poetic, pure bond, was exactly what my heart needed. But enough of this! The main news, the talk of all Moscow, is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Can you imagine! The three princesses received almost nothing, Prince Vasili got nothing at all, and it's Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and has been officially recognized as legitimate—so he is now Count Bezukhov and the owner of the greatest fortune in Russia. People say Prince Vasili played a thoroughly contemptible role in the whole affair and went back to Petersburg completely humiliated.

I'll admit I don't understand much about wills and inheritance, but I do know that ever since this young man—whom we all used to know as plain Monsieur Pierre—became Count Bezukhov and owner of one of the largest fortunes in Russia, I've been greatly entertained watching how the tone and manners of mothers with marriageable daughters, and of the young ladies themselves, have changed toward him. Though, between you and me, he always struck me as a rather unremarkable fellow. Since for the past two years people have amused themselves finding husbands for me—most of whom I don't even know—the Moscow matchmaking rumor mill now speaks of me as the future Countess Bezukhova. But you'll understand I have no interest in that title. Speaking of marriages: did you know that a while ago that universal busybody Anna Mikhaylovna told me, in the strictest confidence, about a marriage plan for you? It involves none other than Prince Vasili's son Anatole, whom they hope to reform through marriage to someone wealthy and distinguished—and you are the one his family has chosen. I don't know how you'll feel about it, but I thought it my duty to tell you. He's said to be very handsome and an absolute rogue. That's all I've been able to find out about him.

But enough gossip. I'm at the bottom of my second sheet of paper, and Mama has sent for me to go dine at the Apraksins'. Read the mystical book I'm sending you—it's an enormous success here. Though there are things in it that are hard for our feeble human minds to grasp, it is a wonderful book that calms and elevates the soul. Farewell! Give my respects to your father and my regards to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you as I love you.
JULIE
P.S. Send me news of your brother and his charming little wife.

The princess sat thinking for a while, a thoughtful smile on her face, her luminous eyes lighting up until her expression was completely transformed. Then she rose abruptly and, with her heavy step, went to the writing table. She took out a sheet of paper and her hand flew rapidly across it. This was her reply, also in French:

Dear and precious Friend, Your letter of the 13th brought me great joy. So you still love me, my romantic Julie? The separation you complain about so bitterly seems not to have had its usual effect on you. You speak of your loneliness—but what should I say, I who am cut off from everyone dear to me? Ah, if we didn't have religion to comfort us, life would be so bleak. Why do you think I would judge your feelings for that young man harshly? In such matters I am strict only with myself. I understand such feelings in others, and though I've never experienced them, I can neither approve nor condemn them. It only seems to me that Christian love—love of neighbor, love of one's enemy—is worthier, sweeter, and more beautiful than the feelings that a handsome young man's eyes can awaken in a romantic and loving young girl like you.

The news of Count Bezukhov's death reached us before your letter, and my father was deeply affected. He says the count was the last representative but one of the great century, and that his own turn is next—though he'll do everything he can to postpone it as long as possible. God spare us from that terrible misfortune!

I can't agree with you about Pierre, whom I've known since he was a child. He always seemed to me to have an excellent heart, and that is the quality I value most in people. As for his inheritance and Prince Vasili's role in it—how sad for both of them. Ah, my dear friend, how terribly true are our divine Savior's words: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of God. I pity Prince Vasili, but I feel even sorrier for Pierre. So young, and weighed down with such wealth—what temptations lie ahead of him! If anyone asked me what I desire most on earth, it would be to be poorer than the poorest beggar. A thousand thanks, dear friend, for the book you've sent, which is enjoying such success in Moscow. But since you tell me it contains things our weak minds cannot understand alongside its good things, it seems rather pointless to spend time on what is incomprehensible and therefore fruitless. I have never understood why some people enjoy confusing their minds with mystical books that only awaken doubt and inflame the imagination, giving them a tendency toward exaggeration entirely contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us read the Epistles and the Gospels instead. Let us not try to penetrate their mysteries, for how can we—wretched sinners that we are—presume to understand the terrible, holy secrets of Providence while we remain in this flesh, which is an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us confine ourselves to the sublime rules our divine Savior left for our guidance here on earth. Let us try to follow them, and let us trust that the less we allow our feeble human minds to wander, the more we shall please God, who rejects all knowledge not from Him; and the less we try to fathom what He has chosen to conceal from us, the sooner He will reveal it through His divine Spirit.

My father has not spoken to me of a suitor, but has only mentioned that he received a letter and is expecting a visit from Prince Vasili. Regarding this marriage proposal, I will tell you, dear sweet friend, that I consider marriage a divine institution to which we must submit. However painful it may be, should the Almighty place upon me the duties of wife and mother, I will try to fulfill them as faithfully as I can, without troubling myself to examine my feelings toward whomever He may give me as a husband.

I've had a letter from my brother announcing his imminent arrival at Bald Hills with his wife. This pleasure will be short-lived, however, as he will be leaving again to take part in this terrible war into which we have been drawn—God knows how or why. Not only where you are, at the heart of affairs and society, but even here, amid farmwork and the tranquility of nature that city people think defines the countryside—here too the rumors of war are heard and felt painfully. My father talks of nothing but marches and countermarches, things I understand nothing about. And the day before yesterday, during my daily walk through the village, I witnessed a heartbreaking scene.... It was a column of conscripts drafted from our people, setting off to join the army. You should have seen the state of the mothers, wives, and children of the men who were leaving. You should have heard the weeping. It seems as if humanity has forgotten the laws of our divine Savior, who preached love and the forgiveness of wrongs—and that people now believe the highest merit lies in the skill of killing one another.
Farewell, dear and kind friend. May our divine Savior and His most Holy Mother keep you in Their holy and all-powerful care!
MARY

"Ah, so you're sending a letter, Princess? I've already sent mine. I wrote to my poor mother," said Mademoiselle Bourienne with a smile, speaking quickly in her pleasant, melodious voice with its rolling r's. She brought into Princess Mary's earnest, sorrowful world a completely different atmosphere—carefree, lighthearted, and self-satisfied.

"Princess, I should warn you," she added, lowering her voice and clearly enjoying the sound of it, speaking with exaggerated affectation, "the prince has been scolding Mikhail Ivanovich. He's in a terrible mood—very grim. Be prepared."
"Ah, dear friend," Princess Mary replied, "I've asked you never to tell me what mood my father is in. I don't allow myself to judge him, and I wouldn't want others to either."

The princess glanced at her watch and, seeing that she was five minutes late starting her practice on the clavichord, hurried into the sitting room with an anxious expression. Between twelve and two o'clock, according to the day's fixed schedule, the prince rested and the princess played the clavichord.
